name: Pump horsepower
seoDesc: Pump horsepower: work out acceleration due to gravity (g) from the discharge and the differential head. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: The Pump horsepower calculator turns the discharge, the differential head and more into acceleration due to gravity (g). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Pump horsepower calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pump horsepower calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports acceleration due to gravity (g) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the discharge (Q), the differential head (H), the density of fluid (ρ) and the efficiency (η).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pump horsepower calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Acceleration due to gravity (g)=efficiency (η) × shaft power (Pₛ) ÷ (density of fluid (ρ) × discharge (Q) × differential head (H))
Shaft power (Pₛ)=hydraulic power (Pₕ) ÷ efficiency (η)
Revolutions (N)=specific speed (Nₛ) × (acceleration due to gravity (g) × differential head (H) ^ 3 ÷ 4) ÷ the square root of (discharge (Q))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Density of fluid (ρ) = 1000 kg/m³, Acceleration due to gravity (g) = 9.81 m/s², Efficiency (η) = 10 . and Hydraulic power (Pₕ) = 10 kW. The calculator returns Shaft power (Pₛ) = 100 kW.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Shaft power (Pₛ) = 100 kW should be roughly the size you expected from Density of fluid (ρ) = 1000 kg/m³ and Acceleration due to gravity (g) = 9.81 m/s².

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in meters per second squared, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilowatts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.
  • Shown in rotations per minute, and convertible to any of the 3 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Flow rate, opening in cubic meters per second
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Rotational speed, opening in rotations per minute
  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • %, opening in decimals
  • Power, opening in kilowatts
  • Power, opening in kilowatts

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pump horsepower calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the discharge, the differential head and the density of fluid — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pump horsepower calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns acceleration due to gravity (g), derived from the discharge, the differential head and the density of fluid. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pump horsepower calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the discharge, the differential head, the density of fluid and the efficiency, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter discharge (Q) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Discharge (Q) opens in cubic meters per second and the chip beside it offers 39 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Shaft power (Pₛ) = 100 kW. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pump horsepower calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
